item.title: Word Duration Directly Cues Word Identity in Mandarin Homophones
item.description:
Word Duration Directly Cues Word Identity in Mandarin Homophones

A new study shows that listeners can use the length of a spoken word to identify it, even when other cues are unavailable.

🔍 Overview

  • The research investigates whether word‑level phonetic cues, specifically word duration, are stored in the mental lexicon and can influence spoken word recognition.
  • Across languages, including Mandarin Chinese, high‑frequency words tend to be shorter than low‑frequency words.

🧩 How it works

  • Researchers used a homophone ordering task with Mandarin Chinese, a language rich in disyllabic homophones.
  • Participants heard pairs of homophones that differed in lexical frequency and were asked to identify the order.
  • The only systematic difference between the stimuli was word duration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Participants reliably mapped the shorter‑duration auditory stimulus to the higher‑frequency word.
  • This mapping held even under high noise levels and when no other cues were available.
  • Results indicate that word duration can serve as a direct cue to word identity, suggesting it may be a phonetic detail incorporated into lexical representations.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides evidence that the mental lexicon stores specific phonetic details (duration) that are functionally relevant for word recognition.
  • Supports a “direct cueing” account of how duration influences lexical access, alongside alternative explanations.

#Psycholinguistics #Mandarin #WordDuration #SpeechRecognition

Source: Direct cueing of word identity through word duration: evidence from Mandarin homophones

item.title: IBM Updates Granite Speech Collection with New Multilingual and High-Speed Models
item.description:
IBM Updates Granite Speech Collection with New Multilingual and High-Speed Models

IBM has announced three updates to its Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model called granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. These models are designed to cover enterprise speech requirements, including high-accuracy transcription, translation, and long-form multi-speaker analysis.

🔍 Overview

Model Primary Use Case Key Attributes
granite-speech-5.0-2b High-accuracy work 2B parameters, multilingual transcription and translation, keyword biasing
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc Raw speed or edge use 470M parameters, 19,870 RTFx speed, native punctuation
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus Meetings and multi-speaker calls Speaker attribution, tighter timestamps, 24% lower long-form WER

⚙️ Key details

granite-speech-5.0-2b

This model is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b and maintains the same parameter count. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio alongside synthetic data for Japanese ASR, translation, and keyword biasing.

  • Multilingual Capabilities: Transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese. Translates to and from English for those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin.
  • Advanced Prompting: Supports Language ID prompting and allows users to request formatted output; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across test sets.
  • Accuracy: Features improved handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Keyword Biasing: Supports lists of up to 2,000 terms to bias transcription toward product names and acronyms.

granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc

Formerly an English-only model, this 470M-parameter encoder is now optimized for speed and multilingual use.

  • Multilingual Expansion: Now supports English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Performance Gains: The model is approximately 1.6x faster than its launch version, reaching 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard by reusing a compiled Conformer block graph.
  • Edge Readiness: Includes native punctuation and capitalization, and supports browser-based streaming via WebGPU.

granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus

This is a drop-in replacement for the original 4.1-2b model, utilizing the same architecture, API, and prompt format with improved weights for long-form enterprise recordings.

  • Speaker Attribution: The word diarization error rate (WDER) and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) both decreased by 7%.
  • Timing Precision: The average timestamp shift (AAS) has been cut by more than half, improving captions and search.
  • Long-Speech Performance: WER on long-form test sets decreased by 24%, while keyword biasing errors fell 45% when using 20-term lists.

🚀 Availability

The models are released under the Apache 2.0 license and include support for:

  • Transformers and vLLM
  • llama.cpp
  • mlx-audio for Apple Silicon

#IBM #Granite #SpeechRecognition #MachineLearning #OpenSource

Source: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

item.title: Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint
item.description:
Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint

Granite Switch 4.1 introduces a family of models that pack chat, decision‑making and speech transcription capabilities into a single endpoint while using roughly the same GPU memory as the base model alone.

🔍 Overview

  • New model variants: Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B and Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B.
  • Each variant bundles three activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters:
    • a Decision aLoRA for general‑purpose decision tasks (e.g., v1/systemone).
    • a Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft‑Decision‑1, GPT‑Luna‑Decisions and Clef‑Flash on safety‑related decision tasks.
    • Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, used for transcription.
  • The combined model occupies approximately the same VRAM as the underlying base model, delivering “more capabilities with fewer GPUs.”

🧩 How it works

  • The adapters are built as cache‑efficient Activated LoRAs. The KV cache generated by the base model during one generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter‑based request.
  • Recent vLLM contributions accelerate low‑rank adapter inference.
  • A co‑located ASR encoder enables the model to switch between chat, decision and spoken requests with “blazing fast speeds.”
  • An example Space – Speech‑to‑Decisions – shows granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribing audio, generating summaries, screening for harmful content and evaluating 15 user‑defined flags in real time on a single endpoint.

⚙️ Key details

Model Size Built‑in adapters
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B 8 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B 30 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
  • Performance: In a “race” against Jev‑27B (frozen Qwen base + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B completed a real‑world, 5‑step RAG workflow faster.
  • Custom use case: A 3 B‑parameter Granite Switch model navigated the classic Doom game at 60–100 decisions / second, compared with Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second, and could also narrate and answer questions while playing.
  • Granite Libraries provide a repository of specialized adapters that can be mixed with the general‑purpose decision adapter at little extra cost because they share the base model’s KV cache.

🚀 Availability

  • The 8B and 30B models are released with “batteries included”, i.e., pre‑compiled with a helpful set of adapters.
  • Users may compose their own Granite Switch models by mixing adapters from Granite Libraries.
  • An Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along with tutorials and support, is planned for future release.

💡 Why it matters

  • Consolidates three major AI functionalities—chat, decision‑making and speech—into one model, simplifying deployment and reducing hardware requirements.
  • Cache‑efficient design and vLLM acceleration make multi‑modal switching real‑time, opening possibilities for interactive applications such as live transcription with instant safety screening.
  • The open‑adapter ecosystem encourages community extensions and custom task specialization without large memory overhead.

#GraniteSwitch #AIAdapters #SpeechRecognition #DecisionModels

Source: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

item.title: Study Improves Child Speech Recognition While Preserving Adult ASR Performance
item.description:
Study Improves Child Speech Recognition While Preserving Adult ASR Performance

Researchers have released an empirical study on adapting automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems for child speech while retaining adult performance.

🔍 Overview

  • Standard ASR models work well for adult speech but often underperform for children and non‑native speakers.
  • Directly adapting adult models to child speech can cause “adult‑speech forgetting,” degrading performance on existing adult benchmarks.

🧩 How it works

  • The study investigates child ASR adaptation with adult retention across Arabic and English.
  • Model families examined:
    • Encoder–decoder (e.g., Whisper)
    • Encoder–CTC
    • AudioLLM‑based ASR
  • Adaptation strategies compared:
    • Full fine‑tuning
    • LoRA (low‑rank adaptation)
    • Post‑hoc weight‑space merging (LERP and TIES)
  • Datasets:
    • Arabic native child speech
    • Arabic non‑native child speech
    • English MyST child speech
    • Adult benchmarks: MGB‑2 (Arabic) and LibriSpeech test‑clean (English)
  • Evaluation metrics: Word Error Rate (WER), Retention Index, Child Adaptation Gain, Adaptation Recovery.

⚙️ Key findings

  • Child adaptation is necessary, especially for non‑native Arabic and English child speech.
  • Direct adaptation often reduces adult ASR performance on the adult benchmarks.
  • Bilingual adaptation (training on both Arabic and English child data) yields a more stable trade‑off than language‑specific adaptation.
  • Weight‑space merging improves the adaptation‑retention balance:
    • Most effective for encoder–CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM models.
    • LERP favours adult retention.
    • TIES recovers stronger child performance gains.
  • For the encoder–decoder model, direct bilingual fine‑tuning remains the strongest approach in raw WER.

📊 Trade‑off details

Adaptation method Effect on adult retention Effect on child gain
Full fine‑tuning May cause adult forgetting Improves child WER
LoRA Less adult impact than full fine‑tuning Improves child WER
Weight‑space merging (LERP) Keeps adult performance higher Moderate child gain
Weight‑space merging (TIES) Slight adult loss Stronger child gain

🚀 Availability

  • Code and pretrained models are released at the provided HTTPS URL (see the original paper).
  • The paper is titled “Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study” and was submitted on 25 Sep 2026 (v1).

#ASR #ChildSpeech #ModelAdaptation #SpeechRecognition

Source: Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study Source: When Forgetting Looks Like Improvement: Metric Masking in Streaming Diarizer Adaptation and the Price of Rehearsal Source: Dialect-Robust Speech Language Models with Synthetic Pseudo-Dialect Augmentation
